title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run declared gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness: the preregistered hypotheses H1/H2 about comparative generator/repair performance were therefore not exercised in this execution (they remain preregistered but unobserved under shared_initial_candidate semantics). We add artifact‑referenced evidence ruling out prompt/response contamination, and we document why repair was not invoked in the archived traces (per‑task parsed_command_count == required_command_count and repair_applied == false for representative tasks). All primary artifacts (execution manifest, per‑task scoring traces, provider calls, and analysis outputs) are archived and referenced in the manuscript evidence bundle.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require both correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, absence of transient safety violations) and flexibility to express diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two architectural approaches are common: (A) translation‑first pipelines that restrict generation to a vendor DSL and apply formal verification/solvers, and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair.

We preregistered the head‑to‑head confirmatory question: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured as deterministic validation: reachability and policy isolation) — (A) translation‑first, or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design with N = 120 paired tasks, gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the validator, and paired_binary_analysis_v1 for analysis. Critically, the preregistration also specified shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired task the orchestration made a single LLM call and supplied the identical textual candidate to both downstream arms. This deliberate design choice removes generator variance from the confirmatory estimand and therefore converts the test into a validator‑acceptance parity experiment for identical candidates rather than an independent generator/repair efficacy comparison. The preregistered hypotheses H1 and H2 (which compare architecture performance under independent generation and repair budgets) were therefore not tested in this execution and remain labeled as preregistered but unobserved under the shared‑candidate operationalization.
sections.related_work: Two research traditions frame our contribution and the experimental axes used here: (1) formal translation and verification systems that prioritize deterministic guarantees (generate inside a DSL and verify with solvers) and (2) LLM‑driven agentic NetOps work that prioritizes flexible generation and iterative repair. Formal translation→verification work (e.g., SymNet, subsequent DSL/NetKAT lines) emphasizes constrained output spaces, solver feedback, and deterministic acceptance decisions; LLM‑centric studies emphasize independent sampling, repair iteration instrumentation, and stochastic robustness. Recent LLM‑agent NetOps work has introduced generate→validate→repair and multi‑agent verifier loops to reduce hallucination and unsafe proposals. Experimental semantics differ importantly: whether generator variance is sampled independently per arm, whether repairs are enabled/instrumented, and whether evaluation focuses on validator acceptance or on generator+repair robustness. Our run intentionally occupies the validator‑acceptance axis under shared candidate semantics and therefore complements prior work that exercises independent generator sampling and repair coverage.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and execution contract. The preregistered plan (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, maximum_model_calls = 240, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. The analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) was fixed (bootstrap percentile CIs and exact McNemar test). The preregistration artifact is archived in the execution manifest.

Task generation and orchestration. Confirmatory tasks (120 pairs) were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each manifest entry contains the intent text, constraints, canonical reference answer, initial and expected final states, and an explicit required_sequence. The orchestration implemented shared_initial_candidate: for each pair the system made a single LLM call and the identical textual candidate was dispatched to both pipeline arms. Execution accounting records model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair) and completed_episode_count = 240 (execution/execution_manifest.json).

Validator, scoring rules, and per‑task artifacts. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, dependency and ordering checks (make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), final state consistency, and produced validation_after.valid (boolean). A per‑task scoring JSON (execution/scoring/task‑XXXX‑*.json) is the canonical evidence for the acceptance decision; these files include normalized_response, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, repair_applied flags, and shared_initial_provider_trace_path which records the exact prompt/response exchange with the hosted model for that pair. Note: the provider call traces referenced by those paths (e.g., execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json) contain the exact prompt delivered to the model and are archived in the execution bundle for independent verification.

Contamination checks and execution isolation. The preregistered contamination procedures were run (held‑out simulator fidelity suite, grammar coverage tests, execution isolation via explicit context reset). The contamination summary (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) contains no flags and the provider audit (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, consistent with execution isolation and with the absence of cross‑task prompt leakage.
sections.results:
Execution and primary statistics. The run completed all preregistered confirmatory episodes: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Analysis (paired_binary_analysis_v1) produced the contingency table n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Marginal success rates were baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0; paired difference A − B = 0.00. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.00, 0.00] and the exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Why repair was not invoked (artifact evidence). Across the archived per‑task scoring traces the repair subsystem was live but never triggered: representative scoring JSONs show repair_applied = false and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true. For example:
• execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, repair_applied = false, validation_after.valid = true.
• execution/scoring/task-000002-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 2, required_command_count = 2, repair_applied = false, validation_after.valid = true.
• execution/scoring/task-000003-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 6, required_command_count = 6, repair_applied = false, validation_after.valid = true.
These concrete per‑task fields (stored in execution/scoring/*.json) explain mechanistically why the repair path was not exercised: each shared candidate satisfied the validator's required_command_count and ordering constraints, so no repair attempts were necessary or recorded. The aggregated condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv) therefore reports successes = 120 and failures = 0 in both arms and repair_applied count = 0 across all episodes.

Contamination diagnostics. Prompt/response contamination was assessed and ruled out in the archived traces: the provider call traces referenced in per‑task scoring JSONs (e.g., execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json; see scoring JSON fields shared_initial_provider_trace_path) record the exact prompt sent to the model for each pair. The task manifest entries show the canonical reference_answer and required_sequence but those fields are manifest inputs to the orchestrator; the provider_calls traces confirm the runtime prompt contained only the intent text and the allowed constraints (not the canonical reference_answer). The contamination summary (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) is empty and provider audit logs show no cross‑condition cache reuse, supporting execution isolation.
sections.discussion:
Measured estimand and interpretation. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics were used, this execution answers a narrow but operationally useful question: given identical LLM candidate proposals, do the downstream translation‑first and agentic orchestration/validation paths differ in deterministic validator acceptance? The artifactized answer is: no — validators accepted the identical candidates in both arms for every paired task (n11 = 120). This is a validator‑acceptance parity result, not a statement about generator sampling, repair coverage, or multi‑model generality.

Why the design produced degenerate concordance. Two jointly artifacted facts explain the degenerate contingency: (1) generation semantics — one shared candidate per pair (model_calls_used = 120) removed generator variance; and (2) candidate quality — the shared candidates matched required sequences and canonical constraints in many cases (per‑task parsed_command_count == required_command_count examples above), so validators accepted them without invoking repairs. Both facts are recorded in the archive and are reproducible from execution/scoring/*.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Implications and actionable protocol changes to test H1/H2. To test the original preregistered hypotheses about comparative generator/repair performance (H1/H2) one must change the generation semantics and resource budget in a follow‑up run: (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent LLM generation per pair (this increases model_calls_used from 120 to 240 for initial candidates as documented in the preregistration), (ii) enable independent sampling or multiple draws per arm to estimate generator variance, and (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations (record nonzero repair_applied flags and repair_provider_trace paths). The preregistration explicitly records these alternative choices and their resource implications; those modifications would create the nondegenerate discordant counts necessary to evaluate H1/H2 and to observe repair coverage.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared_candidate was intentional and improves internal consistency for the validator‑parity estimand but removes generator variance from scope. Construct validity: the binary validator acceptance is a conservative operational gate; richer construct checks (partial correctness, ordering violations) are available in per‑task parsed counts and violation codes archived in execution/scoring/*.json. External validity: the corpus uses Mininet‑derived topologies and synthetically generated tasks and a single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and validator; results do not imply production device equivalence or multi‑model generality. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency yields a point‑mass CI and p = 1.0; all seeds and bootstrap parameters are recorded (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) so results are deterministic and reproducible.
sections.conclusion: We executed a reproducible, preregistered paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks deterministic validators accepted identical LLM candidates in both arms for every pair (n11 = 120), producing paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false across per‑task traces); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage and independent generator robustness were therefore not observed in this execution. The artifact bundle contains per‑task provider calls, scoring traces, the full execution manifest, and analysis outputs; these artifacts support the narrow validator‑acceptance parity conclusion and give a clear, artifact‑grounded path to follow‑up experiments that exercise independent generation and repair instrumentation.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
